title: Who Matters in Coordination Problems?
summary_en: When a planner tries to coordinate many agents on a target action — for example, adopting a new technology — who deserves the largest subsidy? Sákovics and Steiner show that the optimal subsidy structure does not target the 'pivotal' agent in the standard sense; instead it concentrates on agents whose decisions enter many others' best-responses through the network, a property the authors quantify exactly. Their formula tells a planner where the marginal coordination dollar is best spent.
data_used: Theoretical paper. No data; results derived analytically from a global-games / coordination model with heterogeneous agents.
policy_relevance: Practical mechanism-design lesson for Hungarian and EU adoption-subsidy programmes (e-government adoption, electronic invoicing roll-out, SME digital tools, electric-vehicle charging-network installation): subsidy targeting that is calibrated to network influence rather than to need can dramatically lower the public spending needed to hit an adoption threshold. Formula gives a precise way to rank candidate target groups.
